planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or early fall into humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in shade to partial shade; unlike most garden lungworts this European woodland species has plain unspotted green leaves, so grow it for early bloom and texture contrast rather than silvered foliage.

directions: Set divisions in rich, humusy soil under deciduous trees or shrubs where light is dappled in summer and brighter in early spring. Flowers open pink in March and April and age to violet-blue on the same stem, giving a two-tone effect typical of the genus. Leave foliage undisturbed through summer dormancy and water during dry spells to keep the clump from scorching. Divide congested clumps every few years in fall to maintain vigor.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted runners in spring into average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this selection carries heavier silver leaf markings than the species and spreads vigorously by surface runners, so site it where it can be contained by a path, bed edge, or other barrier.

directions: Plant under trees or along shaded walls where its spreading runners can be allowed to roam, since this is one of the more vigorous Lamium relatives and will cross small beds within a season. Whorls of small yellow hooded flowers rise above the heavily silvered leaves in late spring. Shear or mow the planting back once a year to keep foliage dense and fresh looking. Avoid planting near woodland edges where it could escape into adjacent wild areas.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into cool, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; a sport of 'White Nancy' with the same silver leaf center but shell-pink rather than white flowers, it stays compact and is a good choice for small shaded beds or edging.

directions: Tuck divisions into shaded borders or under shrubs where soil stays evenly moist but not waterlogged. Shell-pink flowers appear in whorls from late spring through summer above silver-centered, green-edged leaves. Trim back hard after the first flush of bloom to encourage fresh foliage and a possible rebloom later in the season. Mulch lightly in winter in the colder end of its hardiness range.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant rooted sections in spring into well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; this white-flowered selection is noted for a long, repeating bloom season and a tighter, more compact habit than most Vinca minor forms.

directions: Use trailing stem sections as a weed-suppressing evergreen carpet under trees or along shaded slopes. Pure white, five-petaled flowers open intermittently from mid-spring into early fall rather than in one short burst, giving a longer season of interest than typical blue-flowered forms. Shear lightly after the main spring flush to keep growth dense and encourage repeat flowering. Once established the planting needs little supplemental water except during extended drought.

planting.note: Divide rooted stolons in spring into average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; the cream-splashed foliage of this selection is less vigorous than plain-leaved Waldsteinia ternata, so give it a season or two longer to knit into a solid mat.

directions: Plant along shaded slopes, under shrubs, or as a lawn substitute in heavy shade where the semi-evergreen, cream-marbled leaves brighten the ground year round. Starry yellow five-petaled flowers appear in loose clusters in late spring, resembling a strawberry blossom. The trailing stolons root as they spread, so divide and replant rooted sections to fill in bare patches or start new drifts. Rake away heavy leaf litter in fall so the low foliage is not smothered.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant divisions in spring into average, moist soil in shade to partial shade; variegation holds best out of strong sun, and this trailing mint-family groundcover can spread aggressively, so it is best used in containers, hanging baskets, or beds with a firm edge or barrier.

directions: Grow in hanging baskets, mixed containers, or edged beds where its cream-and-green heart-shaped leaves can trail over the sides without escaping into lawns or wild areas. Small lavender-blue flowers appear in the leaf axils from early spring into early summer. Pinch back runners regularly to keep the planting tidy and to prevent rooting outside the intended area. Lift and divide every couple of years to refresh the planting and control spread.
